en: The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Sulāta, translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Shilun of the Yuezhi state during the Former Liang dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus and five thousand bodhisattvas, the World-Honored One was traveling near the great city of Śrāvastī.
There, kings, ministers, brahmins, elders, and commoners provided for the World-Honored One, supplying him with all that was required.

At that time, there was a man of extreme poverty in the city named Śūradatta. He had faith in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha; he upheld the five precepts and practiced the ten wholesome actions, and while practicing loving-kindness, he never gave rise to a single unwholesome thought.

Toward all sentient beings, he practices compassion with an unwearied resolve; he practices sympathetic joy, always delighting in the True Dharma; he practices equanimity, remaining unmoved by suffering or pleasure; and he maintains a firm, unsurpassed mind set on Right and True Enlightenment. Because he desires to deliver others through skillful means, he dwells in the city of Śrāvastī while manifesting as one who is utterly poor.

Thereupon, Śakra Devānām-Indra, with his pure divine eye, looked clearly upon humanity and saw Sudatta, who was extremely poor in the city of Śrāvastī. He possessed firm and steadfast virtue, and his wholesome conduct was complete and pure; his mind was free from anger. His resolve was firm and strong, without any blemish or impurity. Whether sitting, rising, or walking, he never lost his dignified deportment. In coming and going, moving about, he always maintained equanimity; in eating, drinking, sitting, and lying down, he always harbored an impartial mind. Sleepiness and lethargy were entirely eliminated. He had few desires and was easily contented; he was easily satisfied and easily pleased. He diminished his pursuit of profit, and his mind was unshaken by gain or loss, praise or blame.

With a sincere and steadfast mind, he was free from arrogance; he maintained humility and obedience, his heart was tranquil and pure, and he was upright and eloquent, his speech trustworthy and not flowery. He observed the eightfold fast and knew moderation in eating. He was revered throughout the entire city, never tiring of his presence; and all who came to see him and spoke with him were filled with joy.
He eats sparingly and wears coarse clothing; furthermore, when offerings are presented, he declines and does not accept them.

Using tree leaves as vessels and straw mats as seats, he immediately bestows whatever remains of his food and clothing upon others, storing nothing away for himself. Pure and stainless, he is free from the pursuit of worldly gain, harboring no aspirations toward any form of rebirth.
He constantly visited the Buddha three times each day and night; the Tathāgata always kept his gates open to admit him for prostration, making offerings, and receiving instruction in the Dharma.

Whenever Susīla wished to go to the Buddha, several hundred people would always accompany him. Whether he was traveling, standing, sitting, or lying down in whatever place he dwelt, there was no empty space within that area as it was surrounded by a multitude of people.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra took it to heart and thought:
"This son of noble family possesses pure precepts, refined virtue, and excellent conduct and deportment; I fear he will usurp my position."
"At this moment, try to know and examine closely: what path are you seeking?
Thereupon, Śakra transformed himself into several people who stood before Sūrata and reviled him, speaking words that were contrary to reason.
Furthermore, they sought to harm him with tiles, stones, swords, and staves.
Thereupon, Sūrata, through the power of his patience, practiced a mind of loving-kindness exclusively, remaining without anger or malice.
Then Śakra Devānām Indra again manifested as a man, stood before Sūrata, and said to him:
“Indeed, Sūrata!
Such people as these will revile you without limit, their words contrary to reason, and they will further assault you with tiles, stones, knives, and staves.”
"If you, O Benevolent One, would permit me,
I shall kill him for you. Suruci replied,
"Do not speak such words."

Why is this? Because those who slander others are subject to the retribution of killing; even if they were to cut my body with knives until it was shattered like a *vajra* tree, I would still not harbor ill will toward them.
Why is this so? Because there are two kinds of retribution for all phenomena:
those who plant good seeds are born into the good realms, while those who plant evil seeds fall into the evil realms.
"For this reason, I do not dare harbor resentment toward him, much less desire to take his life.
Thereupon, Sūrata spoke these verses:
"One who plants suffering Will inevitably reap the fruit of suffering."
Whoever plants tranquility will surely produce the fruit of tranquility.
Such a principle of retribution is known as a manifest reality:
for the evil, the retribution is suffering; for the good, the retribution is joy.
Therefore, one should not perform the three unwholesome acts of body, speech, and mind;
for this reason, the wise should not encourage others to do so.
One should always practice the three virtues of body, speech, and mind.
"Always exhort others in this way, if they are those who delight in the good.
Thereupon, the person emanated by Śakra was unable to move Sūrata and so departed.

Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra, before the eyes of Sudrāṣṭra, manifested seven kinds of precious jewels made of gold before him. He further conjured a multitude of people who stood before Sudrāṣṭra and said to him:
"Take these precious jewels; you may use them for giving as alms, or you may cultivate merit;
they can be used for clothing and bedding, or for fine garments, or for delicious food. Why do you persist in this practice of poverty?"
Sudra replied: "O worthy ones!
It is because of my past evil deeds that I have received this retribution, which has made me so poor and lowly today.
Yet, unable to endure this poverty, I would surely commit the act of taking what is not given."
“O Śūradatta! You ought to live joyfully for the remainder of your life; why do you concern yourself with the retribution of future lives and make such talk?
Śūradatta replied:
"O virtuous ones!
This is the dharma of the foolish.
One who perceives the Dharma considers this heavy retribution; one who can consider such heavy retribution is truly wise and discerning."
The person of deluded understanding is stingy and covetous of the possessions of others, thereby committing the offense of taking what is not given;
one who can abandon such stinginess and greed is wise.
Indeed, the unwise person covets much and accumulates it to protect their own life and body; one who has no such protective anxieties is profoundly enlightened.
To perceive permanence in the impermanent, pleasure in suffering, a self in what is non-self, and purity in the impure—such a person commits the offense of taking what is not given.
To contemplate impermanence as suffering, as empty, and as impure is what constitutes true wisdom.
To calculate "me" and cling to one's household constitutes the offense of taking what is not given;
those who do not calculate "me" and do not offend others are wise.
To be never first satisfied and thus remain insatiable constitutes the offense of taking what is not given.
To be content with what one has already received is the mark of wisdom.
One who lacks pure precepts commits the offense of taking what is not given; one whose precepts are pure is wise.
The foolish person, failing to perceive the karmic retribution, commits the offense of taking what is not given; he who perceives the retribution is wise.
Now, those who are greedy and gluttonous commit the offense of taking what is not given; those who are not greedy and gluttonous are wise.
To covet the possessions of others, being arrogant, restless, and agitated, is to commit the offense of taking what is not given; to yield all that one possesses is to be wise.
At that time, he spoke these verses:
"Though hidden treasures amount to a thousand billion, If one has not heard of the mind of renunciation, Such a person is poor in this world; They are not truly wise."
Though one’s household has no store of even a single meal, if one possesses a mind of renunciation and giving,
such a person is truly great wealth, praised by those of wisdom and sagely worth.
When the noble ones clearly manifest themselves, they are able to refrain from doing evil.
The foolish praise what is adorned with ornamentation, yet they do not manifest what is evil.
May I be censured by the wise and not praised by the foolish;
for the foolish praise evil, while the enlightened praise goodness.
The various beings manifested by the deva were unable to cause Sūrata to commit the offense of taking what was not given.
Thereupon, Śakra transformed himself into the form of a householder; holding a superior jewel worth hundreds of thousands, he stood before Sūrata and said to him:
"I have a legal dispute before King Prasenajit, and I am citing you as a witness. I give this jewel to you; I pray that you will bear witness for me."
Sudāsa said to him:
"Virtuous one, do not speak thus; I cannot utter a falsehood out of ignorance. Why is this?..."
One who speaks falsely deceives themselves and deceives others, and deceives all the sages and worthies.
One who speaks falsely causes their own body to emit a foul odor and renders their mind and speech untrustworthy, bringing affliction to their heart.
Now, one who speaks falsely causes their breath to become foul and their complexion to lose its luster; they are forsaken by the celestial deities.
One who speaks falsely loses all roots of goodness; being ignorant and deluded within themselves, they lose the path of virtue.
"Indeed, one who speaks falsely is the root of all evils and the severer of the roots of virtuous conduct and solitary dwelling.
At that time, he spoke these verses:
"When one whose mouth is foul and filthy speaks falsely,"
Having lost the dharma of purity, their will is full of delusions and errors.
Deceived by the gods who protect themselves and led astray by the noble ones,
those men are constantly weak and exhausted.
The root of all evils, wherein the roots of goodness are severed,
will inevitably lead one toward the evil realms.
Even if one were to bestow upon another the entire world filled with gold and pearls, [it would not equal the merit of a single moment of faith].
"One who upholds the Dharma does not speak such words.
Śakra Devānām Indra, unable to make Sūrata speak falsely, then departed.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra addressed the daughter of the Asura, Suyāma, the daughter of King Ādityarāja, and the first lady Viśvakarma-pramukhā, saying:
"Go to the poor Sudhana in the kingdom and disturb his secluded dwelling; test whether he has truly renounced desire or is merely feigning it by practicing asceticism."
Thereupon, Śūrpā, the daughter of the asura king, the daughter of King Divākara, and the foremost lady Viśvāmitrā, at a time of deep night and stillness, went to the place where Sūrata was staying.
He went to him and, speaking with words that were warm and sweet, said to Sudrā:
"Arise, worthy sir!
We have come specifically to serve you."
Moreover, observe us, Sūrata!
Behold our physical forms, so majestic and beautiful, adorned with sandalwood paste, necklaces, and garments, fresh and radiant, at the very height of our prime.
"Śūradatta!
It is by virtue of your merit that you have obtained us as your attendants.
Having looked at them, Śūradatta then spoke thus:
"You all perform the deeds of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals; you do not perform the duties of devas or humans.

Furthermore, observe that your bodies are naturally like illusions and transformations; observe that your forms are like the appearance of gathered foam and bubbles. Even when sandalwood paste is applied to me, I view it in this way. Examine the assembly of dharmas with discernment as impure. Regarding those things that formerly disturbed and defiled you, see them now as such illusory transformations. The mind is restless and its associations are foolish; what is observed is impermanent and subject to dispersal and extinction. By virtue of your own karma, I observe that your conduct leads toward the realms of hell. Thus you have lost your resolve; with the six senses failing to protect your will, how can you be so ignorant and impure? This is precisely what is called craving for desire."
To cling to that which is foul-smelling is to crave desire.
To cling to that which is filthy and evil is to rely upon desire.
To bear all manner of suffering is to crave desire.
Those who crave sensual pleasure are attached to the desire for sense-pleasures.
Those who enter hell are attached to the desire for sense-pleasures.
Those who enter the animal realm are likewise attached to the desire for sense-pleasures.
To enter among the hungry ghosts is to be attached to sensual desire.
To associate with evil people is to be attached to sensual desire.
To fail to accomplish the overcoming of greed is to be attached to sensual desire.
Those who gather for strife, contention, and litigation are attached to sensual desire.
Those who are bound and imprisoned are attached to sensual desire.
Those who give rise to perversions and increase the fetters of craving are attached to sensual desire.
Those who are狂悖 (mad and perverse) and 迷惑 (deluded) are attached to desire.
Those who are 醉亂 (intoxicated and disordered) and 闇冥 (enveloped in darkness) are attached to desire.
That which is frequented by the unwholesome and abandoned by the wholesome, and that which is entangled by all manner of unwholesome things—this is attachment to desire.
Those who lose their way are attached to desire.
Those who practice what is unwholesome are attached to desire.
Those who are weak and inferior, who rob others of their strength, are attached to desire.
That which is covered by clouds is attached to sensual desire;
that which is near to demons is attached to sensual desire;
that which is near to the *pāda-vikṣepa* demon is attached to sensual desire.
To associate with oxen, donkeys, dogs, pigs, camels, elephants, goats, and jackals is to be attached to sensual desire.
To associate with non-human beings is likewise to be attached to sensual desire.
To be devoid of precepts, learning, and generosity is to be attached to desire.
To abandon secluded dwelling is to be attached to desire.
To be exclusively deluded, exclusively obscured, and exclusively burdened by the dust of worldly toil, thereby exclusively diminishing the unsurpassed path, is to be attached to desire.
At that time, he spoke these verses:
"Those who are foul, putrid, and impure, Their desire for decay is likewise so.
Devoted only to suffering and unattached to joy, They dwell in the realms of hell-beings and animals."
Meeting with those who do not digest [their food], and likewise the loathsomeness of desire;
dwelling in places of unrighteousness, with strife, litigation, and malice;
the bonds of bondage, which arise from perversion—these are the things that bind.
That which is increased by sensual desire, and that which arises from it—
this is attachment to desire.
That which is deluded by confusion, and that which accords with and shares in the dust of the world— this is attachment to desire.
The heat of the blazing sun brings together all manner of evils and destroys all that is good; it is the very root of all misdeeds.
Just as the sky is shrouded by clouds, so too is one attached to desire.
Dwelling together with malevolent spirits, The same applies to those who walk on their hind feet;
Deluded by forms and colors, Their craving for sights is likewise so.
Cattle, sheep, dogs, hounds, and pigs, Camels, elephants, rams, and jackals—
Clinging to what is dear to desire, one becomes separated from all dharmas;
whether hearing of giving, combat, or tranquility, one falls away and clings to desire.
Exclusive delusion increases the dust of toil, diminishing the Unsurpassed Way.
This would merely be an attachment to desire.
Even if you were to fill the world, and even if there were those with exquisite beauty surpassing yours,
they could not defile my mind, for all virtues are fully perfected within it.
The asura maiden Śūrpā, the daughter of King Divākara, and the lady of Śikhaṇḍin were unable to move Sūrata;
they all departed and went to Śakra Devendra, saying:
"Having gone to him, do not doubt it."
"Lord of Devas, he has already seen the Truths; there is no longer any female form for him. He has already departed from desire and is entirely unattached to the world.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra was even more struck with alarm and fear, and the hair on his body stood on end:
"There is no doubt about this."
"Noble son, you shall surely be born from me.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra went in person to where Sudhana was; having stood before him with palms joined, he spoke this verse:
"What vow have you made, O Benevolent One, that you practice such a Dharma?"
"Dwelling in seclusion with pure precepts, one becomes the sun, the moon, Śakra, or Brahmā.
Thereupon, Surata replied in verse:
“The sun, the moon, Śakra, and Brahmā—these are the karmic fruits of the three realms. [But] those who dwell in seclusion with pure precepts, They become the sun, the moon, Śakra, or Brahmā.”
All these are impermanent and endure not; they are like the manifestations of an illusion.
How could a person of clear wisdom become attached to the triple world?
That which is without arising or growth is likewise free from old age, sickness, and death.
"Furthermore, he is free from both hatred and love; his state is as level as a scale.
May he bring universal peace to all beings and attain Buddhahood for those who have not yet awakened.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra was filled with joy and leaped for gladness, and a virtuous mind arose within him.

"I exhort you to cultivate a mind of universal compassion; such words as these must be successfully accomplished. May this unsurpassed vow be fulfilled: swiftly subdue all Māras and rain down the nectar of the Dharma for the sake of wandering beings, so that you shall surely become a World-Honored One of universal pity."

Thereupon, at another time, the poor man Śūradatta was walking through the great city of Śrāvastī when he obtained within the city a pearl of the "Auspicious Response of Heaven" (deva-ratna-pratilambha), which had previously belonged to a person and was worth as much treasure as the entire world.
Thereupon, the poor man Sudāna, having taken the jewel, raised his voice and cried out:
"O worthy ones of Śrāvastī!
If there be anyone in this city who is utterly destitute, you should bestow upon them this treasure that is precious to the whole world!"
At that time, former elders and those living in poverty all rushed to him, saying:
"We are utterly destitute; please bestow jewels upon us.
Furthermore, several hundred other people likewise begged me for jewels.
"We are extremely poor," they replied. Sūrata answered,
"You are not poor."
Why is this? Within this great city of Śrāvastī, there is one who is extremely poor; it is to him that these gold and jewel treasures should be bestowed.
The people replied,
"In this city, who is the most impoverished?
He asked again:
"King Prasenajit is extremely poor; you should bestow this treasure upon him.
The people replied, "Stop!
Stop! Sūrata, do not speak such words. Why is this?
"King Prasenajit possesses abundant and vast wealth; his enterprises are widespread, and his granaries and treasuries are overflowing.
Thereupon, the poor Sūrata of the kingdom spoke these verses before the great assembly:
"Though his wealth and enterprises are abundant and extensive, He does not know how to satisfy himself with them."
The great ocean may yet be filled, but this poverty shall never end.
If one increases one's greedy seeking, it will continue on and on without rest;
such is the poverty of the ignorant in both this life and the next.
Thereupon, the poor man of the country, Sudāna, having taken these gold coins and pearls, was surrounded on all sides by a great multitude as he went to King Prasenajit.

At that time, for the sake of his wealth and treasures, King Prasenajit had arrested five hundred eminent sons of noble families and elders, intending to punish them for their crimes and confiscate their property.
Thereupon, the poor man Sudāna took these gold coins and pearls and went to King Prasenajit.
Having arrived, he said to the king:
"While traveling through the great city of Śrāvastī, I obtained these ancient, auspicious, and precious gold coins and pearls, worth as much as the entire world."
"Great King!
I then conceived the thought that I wished to give these jewels to those who were extremely poor.
For this reason, Great King!"
"As I recall, in this city only the King is extremely poor.
Excellent, Great King!
Please accept these jewels."
Thereupon, King Prasenajit felt ashamed and asked the pauper Sudāna,
"Am I poorer than you? Then,
in the presence of the great assembly, the pauper Sudāna spoke this verse to King Prasenajit:
“Those bound by greed increase their karma yet remain unsatiated;
they cause ruin for the king and bring suffering upon themselves as well as others.
Disregarding the next world, devoid of virtue, and heedless of death,”
Is it thus that one is free from greed?
By establishing great compassion well, one does not increase the afflictions of worldly toil;
being content and having no desires, that greed shall never arise again.
If one sees sentient beings, one immediately gives rise to the mind of great compassion;
because of this, there is no resentment or aversion, and thus one is rich in great wealth.
A householder who dwells well in seclusion, and a gentleman who craves wealth and honor—
Just as one who has not attained the Dharma, among those lowly and impoverished beings,
follows all manner of wrong paths, delights in the pleasures of women,
and disregards the world to come— such is the king of these poor ones.
Already belonging to women, their precepts and observances are pure and flawless;
their nature is harmonious and they possess a sense of shame and dread of blame;
having renounced and severed [worldly ties], they dwell in constant peace; hearing the Dharma from the noble sages, they follow it.
When wisdom frequently enters the mind, one abandons the evil realms in future lives.
Such a person is no longer poor; adorning themselves with the Dharma, they never cease the practice of giving by hand, nor do they regard their own life or worldly deeds as essential.
Not following the path toward the essential,
he is like a drunken elephant; such is the poor man,
for he lacks the nature of aspiration.
Revering the Dharma-jewel and the noble assembly, one need not cling to body, life, or karma;
by relinquishing what is non-essential, one easily attains what is essential.
Without anger and without folly, establishing one's resolve in joy and freedom from delusion—such a person is not poor.
Respected by the wise, one does not stop walking even when burned in a dream;
The various streams never reach satiety as they flow day and night into the ocean; The sun and moon are never filled or satiated.
He travels throughout the four quarters; though the king’s greed knows no end, his accumulation of wealth never brings final satiety.
O Great King, one whose nature is fire does not seek to burn grass and wood—this is its constant law.
In this same way, O Great King, you are not burned by the three [fires].
Royal wealth and status are impermanent; they are likened to dew upon the grass.
Who, having heard such a teaching as this, would still long for kingship?
Thereupon, King Prasenajit said to the country pauper Śūradatta:
"I am poorer than you; who shall bear witness to this?
"Does Your Majesty not hear? [he replied.]

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, the All-Knowing and All-Seeing, who has established his realization through verified and sincere knowledge, and who is scrutinized by all the worldlings and asuras, dwells in this great city of Śrāvastī.
“Sūrata! I too have once heard of and seen such a person.
“Great King!”
"The Tathāgata has testified that the king is even poorer than I.
For this reason, Sūrata, you should go and inquire of the Tathāgata; whatever he determines, you should then accept and uphold."
Thereupon, the poor man of the country, Sūrata, spoke these verses:
"My Teacher’s conduct is never at variance; I now reflect upon this:
he knows how to come through the air. There is nothing that he does not know."
Having fully known the minds of both this world and the world beyond,
the Great Sage shall arrive here; he will be free from pride and,
out of compassion for all sentient beings, will surely come even from afar.
Because sentient beings are single-minded in their devotion,
they must maintain faith without weariness; they should establish a vow of utmost sincerity,
for the World-Honored One will surely come.
"With flower garlands and various incenses, banners, streamers, and musical instruments, the Great Sage has thus arrived.
Suḷasa joined his palms, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and spoke this verse:
"If the Buddha truly knows that my resolve is sincere and steadfast,"
"Because of this utmost sincerity, if you know me, stand before me.

Having spoken these words, the earth shook, and the Tathāgata suddenly manifested, emerging from the ground. The five hundred disciples, twelve hundred bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the World-Protectors, along with millions of devas, beheld the Buddha manifesting his supernatural power and marveled at this unprecedented event.

The king, together with his great ministers and all his retinue, knelt and paid homage at the feet of the Victorious One. Thousands of sentient beings made offerings to the World-Honored One, and all resolved their minds upon the Way.
Thereupon, Sudatta, the poor man of the kingdom, joined his palms and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"As I was walking through this great city of Śrāvastī, I obtained a golden pearl of auspicious response from an ancient sage, its value equaling the entire world."
For this reason, World-Honored One,
if there are any who are poor within this city, you should give [the wealth] to them.
World-Honored One!
I consider King Prasenajit of Śrāvastī to be the most impoverished among them. Why is this?

Because he encroaches upon the property of others without knowing contentment; he covets wealth and treasures while disregarding truth and sincerity; he harasses the lowly and the poor to diminish the wealthy; and he is solely intent on royal power and attached to sensual desires.
I gave him this golden pearl, but the King was unwilling to accept it and asked me:
"Is this to testify that I am poor and you are rich in benevolence?

I only wish that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, would—by means of his all-encompassing knowledge and all-encompassing wisdom—examine what is known, examine with faith, and examine with truth, providing a distinct testimony on my behalf."
"Excellent!
World-Honored One!
You maintain an equal mind toward all, having abandoned arrogance and remaining free from partiality; we pray that you will explain this meaning."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:
"Truly so, Great King!
It is exactly as Sūrata has said."
"The World-Honored One truly dwells in such peace.
Thereupon, wishing to resolve the doubts of Śreṇika, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit, saying:
"There is a reason why the Great King is wealthier than Śreṇika, and there is a reason why Śreṇika is wealthier than the Great King."
What are the conditions for this?

They are the royal affairs and the benefits of noble status: the retinue, gold, silver, pearls, jade, crystal, lapis lazuli, and genuine pearls; coral, elephants, horses, carriages, and storehouses filled with precious treasures. It is by these causes and conditions that the Great King is more wealthy than Sudāsa.
Furthermore, Great King!

By virtue of the qualities of generosity, ethical discipline, learning, renunciation, non-attachment, and dwelling in seclusion; by compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; by meditative concentration, liberation, samādhi, and right attainment; by firm resolve in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha; and by upright faith, a sense of shame, and conscientious conduct—for these causes and conditions, Great King!
Sūrata is more wealthy than the king.

Even if all the people under the Great King’s jurisdiction were as rich in wealth and treasures as the Great King himself, they would not equal one hundredth, nor one thousandth, nor even a hundred millionth part of the conduct, observance of precepts, learning, generosity, and wisdom of this noble Sūrata in the interval of his seven steps. They cannot be compared to him.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit, having set aside his pride, addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"I have gained a most excellent benefit and dwell in peace, for within my realm there is such a Great Being."
The World-Honored One said:
“So it is, Great King! So it is, Great King!”
"Within the realm of Your Majesty, there is this Great Being.
Furthermore, O Great King!
Moreover, there are many other Great Beings in the kingdom who are like Sūrata."
King Prasenajit spoke these verses before Sūrata:
"You are my teacher, and the Buddha is also my teacher;
because of you, I have abandoned my arrogance, and I now bestow upon you the office of Prime Minister."
I pray that I may accompany you and your retinue to become your disciples.
Deceived by arrogance, I have been led through this long night;
deluded by the pursuit of royal power, I have not practiced the Way of the Dharma.
Now that I have heard the words of Sūrata, I shall practice the Dharma out of my devotion to your virtue.
These five hundred men were bound by me because of greed;
I now release them all and offer myself as your servant and attendant.

Having heard this and attained liberation, these five hundred people wished to repay the kindness of Sulabha; they extinguished their worldly intentions and disregarded karma, no longer looking back toward conditioned responses, and made a solemn vow to establish the mind of omniscience.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit said to Sūrata:
“I am poor, while you, O virtuous one, are not poor.
What you have said, O virtuous one, is truly excellent.”
"As for this one called Sudhana, though he was exiled for violating the king’s law, he should simply be named Sudhana; he must no longer be called 'Poor'.
Thereupon, the noble son Sudhana rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This great assembly has gathered everywhere, desiring to see the Tathāgata."
Excellent,
World-Honored One!
For the sake of this great assembly, you have thus expounded the Dharma, causing this great assembly not to forget the sight of the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed Sūrata, saying:
“Noble son! If a noble son or noble daughter who sees the Tathāgata is endowed with and upholds four dharmas, they see him truly and see him well.”
What are the four dharmas?
A sincere mind, an affectionate mind, a joyful mind, and a respectful mind—these are the four.
"Furthermore, there are four more."
"What are the four? Suḷata!

When sons or daughters of good family behold the perfected physical form of the Tathāgata, they immediately resolve their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; with a sincere heart they resolve their intentions, never deviating from the intent of the Tathāgata."
Because he cherishes sentient beings and desires to deliver them forever;
because he desires to cause them to uphold the Dharma;
and because he desires to ensure that the Three Jewels are never interrupted.
“By means of these four dharmas, Sūrata!
sons of good family and daughters of good family fully perceive the Tathāgata, achieving that which is called thorough perception and excellent perception.

Furthermore, there are four other dharmas by which sons of good family and daughters of good family perceive the Tathāgata, achieving that which is called thorough perception and excellent perception.”
What are the four?

One does not perceive anything within the formations of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; one contemplates the four great elements as equal to emptiness and all sense-faculties as like an empty village, yet one maintains the awareness of the notion of "self."
By these four matters, sons and daughters of good family achieve their refined vision and excellent insight.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which sons and daughters of good family perceive the Buddha as utterly pure:

purity through being free from the self because of having left the self behind; purity through being free from sentient beings because of having left sentient beings behind; purity through being free from the life-principle because of having left the life-principle behind; and purity through being free from the vital span because of having left the vital span behind.
By being fully endowed with these four dharmas, sons and daughters of noble family perceive the Tathāgata as exceedingly pure.
Furthermore, there are four others.
What are these four?

The divine eye is characterized by non-action; the wisdom eye is characterized by non-attachment in practice; the Buddha-eye is like thorough awakening; the Dharma-eye is like knowing that which appears—these are the four dharmas.
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas by which sons and daughters of good family perceive the Tathāgata as utterly pure.
What are these four?

Purity in the category of ethical discipline (*śīla-skandha*), being unattached to anything; purity in the category of meditative concentration (*samādhi-skandha*), because all dharmas are established through concentration; purity in the category of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*), because of the equality of supramundane knowledge; and purity in the category of the vision of the knowledge of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-skandha*), because of being well-liberated and liberated such that there is nothing further to be transcended.”
"Because these four dharmas are fully possessed, one sees the Tathāgata as utterly pure.

While this sequential teaching of the Dharma through these four matters was being spoken, seven hundred disciples resolved their minds [on liberation], attaining deliverance by means of the vehicle of the disciples; and a full thousand beings resolved their minds on the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One preached this Dharma instruction for King Prasenajit and the great assembly, causing them all to rejoice and exult. He then rose from his seat and, together with the Bodhisattvas and the great disciples, traveled through the air by means of his supernormal power like a king of geese, returning to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit addressed the noble son Sudrāta, saying:
"When you, O virtuous one, go to the Tathāgata, I pray that you will inform me; it would be well if I might serve as your attendant."
At that time, the king also made a vow: "The ladies of the Great King’s inner palace, as well as the various ministers and the great assembly, shall all go together to see the Buddha.
Thereupon, within the great city of Śrāvastī, he established a universal decree: anyone who did not go to the Buddha would be subject to punishment.
Why is this so? Furthermore, Great King, it is because a bodhisattva’s practice is not established for his own sake alone;
rather, a bodhisattva’s practice is established with the desire to bring peace and security to all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Great King!
A bodhisattva does not resolve upon the path for the sake of one person or two persons; rather, he assembles a great multitude to serve as his retinue, thereby manifesting excellence.
He asked again:
"What is meant by the 'retinue' of a bodhisattva?
[The Buddha replied: "All beings are the retinue of a bodhisattva, because he desires to deliver and liberate them."
The generation of the aspiration for enlightenment is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it does not remain in the Lesser Vehicle but advances further.
Firmness of mind is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it seeks to subdue all deceitful sentient beings.
A mind free from attachment is the escort of a bodhisattva, for it causes one to advance by adhering to extraordinary conduct.
A mind free from hesitation is the escort of a bodhisattva, for it does not stop at mere equanimity but continues to progress.
The mind of generosity is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it gathers in those sentient beings who harbor envy.
The mind of ethical discipline is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it gathers in those sentient beings who possess faulty morality.
The mind of patience is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it gathers and sustains those beings who are restless and agitated.
The mind of diligence is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it gathers and sustains those beings who are indolent and remiss.
The mind of meditative concentration is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it gathers and sustains sentient beings whose minds are distracted.
The mind of wisdom is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it gathers and sustains sentient beings who possess all manner of unwholesome knowledge.
"O Great King! Loving-kindness is the retinue of this bodhisattva, because the mind dwells upon never abandoning sentient beings.
Compassion is the retinue of this bodhisattva, because one enters into birth and death without weariness or aversion."
A mind of joy is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it gladdens sentient beings with the delight of the Dharma.
A mind of protection is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it practices equanimity by extinguishing both hatred and attachment.
"O Great King! These four debts of gratitude are the retinue of a bodhisattva, for they practice equally with all phenomena that have no fixed abode.
The various roots of goodness and their karmic retributions are the retinue of a bodhisattva, for they are fully endowed with the marks and signs of excellence and wisdom."
The purification of vows is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it purifies the buddha-fields.
The three gates of liberation are the retinue of a bodhisattva, because they constitute the equal practice of dwelling within the gate of the deathless.

Sincerity and faithfulness, refraining from double-tongued speech, harsh words, false speech, and frivolous talk are the retinue of a bodhisattva, for they consist of practices that do not involve contradictory or offensive language.
Gentle and sweet speech is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it accords with eloquent responses and similar practices.
Freedom from disturbance is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because one never displays an unseemly countenance toward any sentient being.

To be fully endowed with extensive learning and to transform what has been relinquished into what is received is the retinue of this bodhisattva, because of the non-forgetfulness and equanimity of his resolve and mindfulness.
To revere teachers and elders is the retinue of this bodhisattva, because he causes others to hear the Dharma not yet heard and upholds the true Dharma by practicing it.
The mind of renouncing the household life is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it acts as an equal practice that is never diminished.
The mind of dwelling in seclusion is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it firmly guards both the white and black dharmas.
The mind of dignified deportment is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it does not expect to receive anything from others.
Pure virtue free from defilement is the retinue of a bodhisattva, for it practices with roots of goodness that are sweet and equal.
A pure mind is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it establishes faith and the practice of equal conduct in sentient beings who lack it.
A mind free from indulgence is the retinue of a bodhisattva, because it brings to full completion and fulfillment all the factors of enlightenment and the practices of equal conduct.

Thereupon, King Prasenajit, having heard these words, was filled with joy and exultation; a virtuous mind arose within him. He offered to Sūrata fine garments and upper robes of various colors, worth hundreds of thousands [of coins], saying:
"For the sake of making offerings to the Dharma, receive this for the sake of the Dharma."
He was unwilling to accept it and spoke these words:
"Stop! Stop!"
"Great King!
This is what the king wears. Why is that? Because—"
"I myself possess worn garments made of patched rags.

At times, Great King, these worn garments of mine are hung upon a tree for one day or even up to seven nights; yet no one takes them, nor does anyone covet them, and I set out on my wanderings without any sense of regret or attachment."
"For this reason, Great King!
As for clothing, it serves merely to cover the body; it should cause oneself to be free from attachment and prevent others from being covetous.
King Prasenajit then addressed the noble son Sudra, saying:
"If you, Sūrata, will not accept this robe, I pray that you will step upon it with your feet, so that I may obtain merit and peace for a long night.
Thereupon, the noble son Sūrata, out of compassion for King Prasenajit, caused his foot to tread upon this garment worth hundreds of thousands.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit said to the noble son Sudrāṭha,
"Regarding these famous garments that you have trodden upon with your feet, what do you intend to do with them?"
He replied: "Great King!
These garments are known as 'name-cloths'; there are many who are poor, destitute, and solitary within the city of Śrāvastī to whom they may be given."
Thereupon, King Prasenajit commanded his attendants and ministers to take the robes and go into the city of Śrāvastī to bestow them upon those who were poor, destitute, solitary, or frail with age.
“Yes, indeed, Great King!

Thus did the various people of the kingdom and those who were poor hear that King Prasenajit had given a garment worth hundreds of thousands, of many different colors, to Sūrata, bestowing it as a gift.
From within and without the city, beings gathered everywhere in Śrāvastī; hundreds of billions of sentient beings, having each obtained these garments worth hundreds of thousands, all put them on.
Once he had finished putting on his robes, a virtuous thought arose in him:
"With what should I repay this Sūrata and offer him worship?
Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and established by Sūrata himself, a voice then manifested in the air, saying:
"One cannot repay Sūrata with incense, flowers, or unguents, nor with sweet delicacies; there is nothing that surpasses the arousal of the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).

Sūrata does not act for the sake of food or clothing, nor for the sake of profit, offerings, praise, or fame; he acts solely for the sake of liberating sentient beings and arousing the aspiration for enlightenment. Those who comply with his teaching should practice the wisdom of the Path."

Thereupon, the noble son Sūrata rose from his seat and, together with King Prasenajit, surrounded by the ladies of the harem, court beauties, ministers, officials, and a great multitude of people before and behind him, departed from the city of Śrāvastī and proceeded to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

Within the great city of Śrāvastī, there were ten billion people, including the poor of the land; hearing that the son of good family Sudhana was going to see the Tathāgata, they all followed him out of remembrance of Sudhana’s kindness.

By the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, Śakra Devānām Indra traveled from the city of Śrāvastī to the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden; along the way, he manifested a ceremonial ground that was vast, adorned with various colorful and exquisite decorations, like the Sudharmā Hall of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

Furthermore, he manifested various kinds of jewel trees, and beneath each tree he manifested a lion throne, exquisite, sublime, and solid, a thousand cubits in height, draped with hundreds of thousands of celestial silks embroidered with variegated colors.

The daughter of the asura, the consort of Śūrya, together with ten thousand jade maidens, all attended and guarded him; they all held celestial flowers, celestial incense, drums and music, and stringed songs, making offerings to the Tathāgata’s lion throne, having thus completed their worship.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One, knowing that the assembly had gathered, went forth from the Jeta Grove together with the bodhisattvas and great disciples, proceeding to the majestic and pure lion throne.
Having arrived, he sat cross-legged upon the lion throne.
As soon as the Tathāgata sat upon the lion throne, this trichiliocosm shook in six ways, manifesting eighteen auspicious omens—shaking, shaking again, and shaking most violently.

At that time, the son of Śakra-devānām-indra, Gautamīputra, was seated among the assembly. Thereupon, the devaputra Gautamīputra manifested sixty thousand seats. Once the manifestation by the deva was complete, he invited the bodhisattvas to each take a seat and spoke these verses:
"May the pure ones sit; the sages shall sit upon these seats. These seats are the root of goodness;
one will swiftly attain the seat of Buddhahood."
Out of compassion for the devaputra Ghoṣila, the bodhisattvas sat upon their seats.
Thereupon, the prince Prajñājñānabuddhi said to the princess Divyagati:

"Go, together with these five hundred celestial musicians, sing in unison in praise of the Buddha’s virtues and jointly make offerings to the World-Honored One at his lion-throne until the time when Sūrata arrives."
Why is this? Noble son, the merit of Sūrata is so lofty and his retinue so vast that those who would see the Tathāgata will not recognize you all.

Then the princess Divākara-carī, the consort of Prince Prajñā-jñāna-kṣema-dhara, performed five hundred musical pieces and approached the Tathāgata. Having arrived, they all prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; holding their musical instruments in their hands, they all praised the virtues of the World-Honored One with a single voice, singing this hymn:

“The World-Honored One, in the past, cultivated the practice of solitary dwelling for a hundred kalpas. The World-Honored One universally harmonizes sentient beings, causing them to delight in giving. The World-Honored One’s body, speech, and mind delight in upholding the pure precepts. We vow to pay homage to your body, which is like Mount Sumeru.”

The World-Honored One’s patience and compassion are steadfast and effortless; the World-Honored One’s vigor is firm and powerful like a tree; the light of the World-Honored One’s divine wisdom accomplishes all things—may I pay homage to the one who is stainless despite the three defilements.

The World-Honored One has already triumphed over the defilements of lust, hatred, and delusion; the World-Honored One has accomplished all that was to be done. We pray to pay homage to the one who is worthy of offerings throughout the three realms.
When these defiled māra-maidens were seen by the Tathāgata, their minds attained peace through their stainless eyes.

Having accomplished mindfulness of the Buddha and abandoned desire, they no longer approach or touch upon desire; they delight in questioning the Tathāgata on how to remove the stains of the mind. May those who possess weary and stained thoughts find joy in the minds of the assembly; I pray that you pay homage at his feet.

Training the world through two hundred superior marks, adorned with necklaces of a hundred merits and virtues fulfilled, your sublime voice purifies wherever sentient beings go; I vow to pay homage to you, the incomparable deity beyond reach.
Divine and celestial, with feet as soft as gold, you walk with the gait of a lion amidst clouds;

having been born from a womb for the sake of transforming those you encounter, your praised virtues are now perfected by a hundred blessings. May you cause the minds of all sentient beings to be universally joyful and free from weariness; may those who praise your supreme virtues swiftly attain that which they praise.

Thereupon, the noble son Sudāsa, together with King Prasenajit and the king’s harem, surrounded by a great multitude of followers and praised by hundreds of thousands of devas, proceeded to where the World-Honored One was. Having arrived, he prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One and stood to one side.
King Prasenajit bowed his head at the feet of the Tathāgata, circumambulated him three times each, and stood to one side.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit offered his own seat to Sūrata and spoke these words:
"O son of noble family!..."
"Out of grace and compassion, please sit upon this seat of benevolence.
Sudāna then sat upon that seat of benevolence.
Thereupon, among the assembly, there were certain sons of gods who had not yet seen Sudāna; they wondered what merit this poor man possessed such that he was so honored and respected by the King.
Thereupon, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing the thoughts of the sons of the gods, addressed them, saying:
"Do not give rise to conceited thoughts regarding these worthy ones, lest the merit of you all be diminished and you remain in unrest for a long night."

Why is this? It is because I have clearly discerned that this son of noble family is filled with great merit and wholesome dharmas; furthermore, O sons of the gods, wait but a moment and observe how his merit and wholesome dharmas are fully perfected.
Thereupon, the noble son Sūrata, wishing to gladden the hearts of the devaputras, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“So be it, World-Honored One!

You have now spoken of the majesty of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s deliverance of sentient beings, the majesty of his wisdom, and the majesty of his manifestations—all fully perfected and complete—by which he swiftly achieves the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.”
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a radiance from his body such that it illuminated the body of Sudāna.

As soon as it touched his body, the noble son Sudāna was graced by the Buddha’s light; at that moment, Sudāna’s body surpassed that of Śakra, Lord of the Devas, by many thousands of millions of times, and Sudāna’s body became so exceedingly beautiful.

Thereupon, the sons of the gods, seeing that Sūrata’s body was so exceedingly beautiful, were filled with great joy; they prostrated before Sūrata and scattered heavenly flowers over him in reverence.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the son of good family, Sudrāṣṭra, saying:
"When a bodhisattva dwells in nobility yet manifests in lowliness, it is because he desires to deliver sentient beings; this is what is called the adornment and purification of wisdom."
Furthermore, one delights sentient beings through dignified conduct; having delighted them, one then manifests one's practice and long-standing supernatural powers—this is the purity of wisdom.
Moreover, son of good family!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains mastery over his mind and manifests as one who is extremely poor, yet he is revered by all the brahmins and the people; this is what constitutes adornment and purification.
Furthermore, son of good family!

If a bodhisattva manifests as poor and lowly to inspire those of external paths and eliminate their greedy intentions; or manifests as engaged in great worldly affairs, and then again manifests as having left the household life, desiring thereby to guide and instruct sentient beings who are weary of the household—that is what constitutes adornment and purification.
This, Su-lai, is the Bodhisattva’s purification of sentient beings;
it is the fulfillment of the equipment of purified wisdom and purified vigor, by which one swiftly achieves the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Thereupon, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“This son of good family has been practicing for a long time; why is it that he has been so adorned by the Tathāgata?”
Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Ānanda, this son of noble family, in past ages, fully provided offerings to many hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas.

He practiced the deeds of the various *pāramitās*, taking supernatural powers as his sport. Having attained the three kinds of patience (*kṣānti*) and having attained appropriate eloquence (*pratibhāna*), he skillfully delivers sentient beings through expedient means; therefore, he manifests as one who is extremely poor."
Thereupon, Ānanda addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How many are the noble sons such as Sudāna who manifest the conduct of poverty to deliver sentient beings?"
The World-Honored One told Ānanda:

"Seven thousand gods of the desire realm and twelve thousand gods of the form realm have all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; furthermore, countless worldly people who have resolved their minds upon the path and those born in auspicious realms [have likewise attained this]."
He asked again:
"After how long will you attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path?
What will your name be when you have attained that path?"
"What is the nature of that Buddha-world’s adornment and purity?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, wishing to praise the noble son Sūrata for the adornment and purity of his land, spoke these verses:
"Ānanda, listen as I extol The guides of all worlds."
Because of bringing sentient beings to fulfillment, his name is praised as lofty, vast, expansive, and universal;
having set forth on the practice of the Mahāyāna, his kalpas have been infinite in number.
From the very first moment he resolved his mind, since the time he began practicing virtuous deeds, [he has remained thus].
Serving all Buddhas and that which they offer;
because one constantly protects the elders of all dharmas,
wherever wisdom proceeds, it acts within the various pāramitās.
Delighting in the superknowledges, practicing the four immeasurables through the long night,
well-trained in skillful means, seeing the defilement of birth and death,
discerning clearly the Buddha-dharma, and well-versed in the purity of marks—
Knowing the fundamental nature of sentient beings, he delivers them according to that nature.
Through the practice of mental wisdom, he abides in profound purity;
having attained eloquence suited to the capacity of others, he dwells in all the dhāraṇīs.
Having already crossed over the hook of Māra, the majestic deportment of all Buddhas,
Firmly abiding and unmoving, without defilement or attachment,
He has transcended the eight worldly dharmas; gain and loss appear as total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
Regarding all phenomena, there is nothing [to grasp]; neither distant nor near, like the nature of empty space, their minds are without attachment.
Without a sense of weariness or fatigue, they constantly practice the mind of great compassion.
Firmly established in dhāraṇī, clad in the armor of compassionate virtue;
as one treats oneself with kindness, so does one toward all sentient beings,
never harboring resentment or malice, nor seeking retribution against those who offend.
As it is appropriate to receive, one welcomes it without avoidance;
speech and action do not contradict one another. One universally studies all dharmas according to the characteristics of liberation;
through these two dharmas, one is liberated from both.
Fully endowed with the three kinds of patience, they give rise to nothing in their conduct.
This is the practice of all Buddhas; they establish themselves well in dignified deportment.
Practicing throughout all lands, they bring great benefit to sentient beings.
That direction is not fixed, and there is no Tathāgata there;
yet wherever Sūrata goes, it is as if one were making offerings to the World-Honored One—
reverence should likewise be shown to him by all devas and worldly people.
After my parinirvāṇa, when the Dharma is on the verge of extinction in future ages,
Sulabha shall practice there in the world-system of the East;
that land is named Wondrous Bliss, and the Tathāgata there is named Unwrathful.
When returning from that place, the remaining three asaṃkhyeya kalpas shall not be diminished in their number.
One should continue to diligently practice the Path and adorn and purify the buddha-field.
Out of a desire to deliver sentient beings, he shall, after this kalpa, attain the supreme path; his name shall be King Avalokiteśvara.
His land shall be like that of Akṣobhya Buddha, a world such as that of the Tathāgata.
The world is named Well-Transformed (Suvikrānta).
He dwells there with a lifespan of ten thousand years, remaining in the world to teach and transform.
The number of monks is beyond measure; those who give rise to the Lesser Vehicle are few.
Seeking the infinite Great Vehicle, they universally know the power of spiritual penetrations;
for the foolish, ignorant, and defiled common folk, they skillfully transform them until all are pure.
They shall cause all to be praised, teaching and instructing through the transformation of the single Dharma.
He shall be free from the entanglements of Māra; his pure wisdom shall be universal and equal.
After he guides the world to parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma shall remain in the world for eighty-four thousand years, and the wisdom of the Dharma shall not be hidden.
"The assembly transformed by Sūrata shall follow his lofty path and conduct;
all shall be reborn there, with the exception of those who have exhausted their outflows.

While he was thus explaining and resolving the matter for the noble son Sūrata, each member of the entire assembly covered Sūrata with their robes, and the sound of their encouragement was heard throughout the entire trichiliocosm.

By the sound of that exhortation and support, immeasurable and innumerable devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all arrived at the sound, gathered together and sat down, making offerings to the son of good family, Sudrā.
The World-Honored One also, for their sake, preached various teachings based on these causes and conditions of the Dharma, causing them all to clearly understand the practices of the Three Vehicles.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit stood before the World-Honored One, joined his palms, and addressed the World-Honored One:

"I was intoxicated by the throne of kingship; intoxicated by wealth and enterprise; intoxicated by honor and nobility; and intoxicated by my treasuries of gold, silver, granaries, and grain. Greedy and insatiable, I oppressed sentient beings to serve as the state's resources."
"World-Honored One, in every lifetime,
when I have practiced the Dharma through such positions and stations as these, it was always after hearing them from the noble son Sudrāṣṭra that I was resolved by Sudrāṣṭra, who is utterly poor."

"Now, before the World-Honored One, I renounce my kingdom and establish Prince Vairāṭa as the crown prince; I shall observe the precepts and offer myself, serving as a gardener and attendant for the World-Honored One and the assembly of monks."
All wealth and treasures should be divided into three portions:
one portion to be offered before the Buddha to the Saṃgha;
two portions to be given to the poor, the destitute, and the solitary.
One-third is set aside as a reserve for the affairs of state.
Who then, World-Honored One,
having heard such a teaching regarding the station and rank of the Dharma, would still harbor attachment to wealth and worldly occupations?
Those who are possessed by ignorance and evil friends harbor such attachments;
I shall dedicate these roots of goodness performed by me to sentient beings, wishing that they may resolve to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

Thereupon, five hundred elders, five hundred householders, five hundred brahmins, and five hundred officials within the assembly, having heard King Prasenajit utter such a lion’s roar, all conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment; they abandoned their households, wealth, and occupations, desiring to leave the home life and enter the path under the transformational influence of the World-Honored One.
He placed three hundred people in the center, while the remainder all appeared as bhikṣu-saṃghas, having already shaved their hair and beards and donned the kāsāya robes.

Thereupon, the son of good family Sudrāra rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the World-Honored One, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I pray that I may receive the renunciation of the household life from the World-Honored One and from all the Buddhas currently present in the ten directions.”
Thereupon, the noble son Surata prostrated himself before the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the ten directions, and made this vow:
"May the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, grant me permission to enter the Way."

Thereupon, each of the Buddhas extended his right hand and stroked Sūrata’s head; as soon as their hands touched his head, his beard and hair all fell away, the dharma robes were donned upon his body, and his majestic deportment became composed and serene.

Thereupon, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways; a great radiance was emitted, universally illuminating the ten directions, and celestial flowers rained down, such that the arms of all these Buddhas did not obstruct one another.
The World-Honored One Śākyamuni extended his golden arm and stroked the head of Susīla, saying:
"Those who have resolved to attain the Way and behold this manifested transformation shall all receive the prediction of their future enlightenment from the Buddhas."

When this Dharma was being taught, five hundred bhikṣus who had set out upon the vehicle of the disciples all attained non-attachment, and a full thousand bodhisattvas all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Elder Ānanda, saying:
"Receive this Dharma transformation, uphold it, recite it, and explain it extensively to the great assembly of sentient beings."
Why is this so? Because this is an age of five turbidities:

the turbidity of sentient beings, the turbidity of afflictions and defilements, the turbidity of lifespan, the turbidity of false views, and the turbidity of the kalpa. It was not the time for a Buddha to appear in the world; therefore, wishing to deliver such beings, Sūrata manifested as one who is utterly poor.
Why is this? It is not because of the conditions of this Sahā world-system that I fail to manifest the liberation of even a single person.
For this reason, Ānanda!
When manifesting this Dharma to instruct sentient beings, these sentient beings shall believe in this Dharma and shall attain liberation; they shall be thus transformed by the Tathāgata.
The Buddha told his disciples:
“Hold this well in mind with virtuous reflection.

When the noble son Sudatta, King Prasenajit, Śakra-devānām-indra, the Elder Ānanda, the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, and the people of the world heard what the Buddha had spoken, there was none who did not rejoice; they bowed their heads in prostration and departed.
The Sūtra Spoken by the Buddha on Sulabha (or Śūradatta)
